---
title: "Chunking"
description: "The process of dividing content into smaller units for storage, processing, or retrieval."
term: "Chunking"
letter: "C"
category: "Retrieval"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

Chunking divides a larger document or input into smaller pieces. In
retrieval systems, these pieces can be indexed and selected independently
instead of searching or sending an entire collection at once.

## Technical explanation

A chunking strategy defines boundaries and sizes, often using tokens,
sentences, paragraphs, or document structure. Choices include fixed-size
windows, semantic boundaries, and overlapping chunks. Chunk size and
overlap affect retrieval precision, context completeness, index size, and
the amount of text passed to a model.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Retrieval-augmented systems rely on useful units of text to index and
retrieve. Poor chunk boundaries can separate a claim from its context,
produce irrelevant matches, or exceed the model's context budget.

## How it works

The source is parsed, divided according to a chosen strategy, and each
chunk may retain metadata such as document identity, section, and
position. Chunks are then indexed or supplied to downstream components.
The strategy should be evaluated on the actual retrieval task.

## Practical example

A handbook can be split by headings and paragraphs, with a small overlap
between adjacent chunks when a section boundary might separate related
sentences. Retrieved passages can then be traced back to the original
section.

## Common misconceptions

- Smaller chunks are not always better; they may lose necessary context.
- Overlap can preserve continuity but also increase duplicate retrieval
  and storage.
- Chunking does not itself make source content accurate or retrieval
  relevant.
